classical

/KLASS-ih-kuhl/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Classical means relating to a long-established formal style regarded as a standard of excellence, such as ancient Greek and Roman art and culture.

The architect designed the new courthouse in a classical style, with tall columns and a triangular pediment echoing ancient Rome.

Example

Rather than composing an entirely modern score, the film's composer chose a classical structure for the main theme — a full orchestra, a clear melodic line, and formal movements — deliberately evoking symphonies written two centuries earlier.

The composer wasn't inventing a brand-new musical form; he was drawing on a long-established tradition treated as a model of excellence, which is exactly what "classical" describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

canonical: Canonical means treated as an official model or standard that everyone in a field is expected to know — the canonical texts, the canonical repertoire. Classical is broader and older in flavor: it ties excellence to a long-established style, like Greek and Roman art, rather than to an official list.

formal: Formal describes work that follows set structures and rules — a formal essay, a formal garden. Classical adds prestige to that structure: a classical form is not just rule-governed but honored as a standard of excellence built over centuries.

timeless: Timeless says something never goes out of date — its appeal doesn't depend on any era. Classical makes a different claim: the thing belongs to a long-established tradition regarded as a standard of excellence. A plain white shirt is timeless; a symphony's form is classical.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

modern: belonging to the present or recent era, rather than tradition

avant-garde: experimental and ahead of its time, the opposite of established tradition

Where it sits · how much it sets the standard

traditional → time-honored → classical

traditional vs. classical: A traditional recipe has simply been passed down through a family or culture; classical claims far more — a form held up as the very model of excellence.

time-honored vs. classical: Time-honored is weaker than classical: a time-honored recipe has earned respect by surviving, but a classical form goes further, standing as the very standard of excellence others are measured against.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — class-: a group or division (Latin classis)

Suffix — -ic: relating to — this much on its own already spells a word: classic

Suffix — -al: relating to, again — a second adjective ending on top of classic, already a word by itself. English pairs -ic and -al so often that -ical reads as one familiar ending.

Put it together: "classical" builds on class-, originally referring to a defined social rank; over time, the "classical" writers and artists of ancient Greece and Rome came to represent the top, most esteemed rank of cultural achievement — hence "classical" now means belonging to that standard-setting tradition.

Use the root in a new word: classify: Librarians classify each new book by subject before shelving it.
